items.text: Most teams jump straight to Agentic AI frameworks. Then wonder why their agent works in demos but breaks in production. The framework isn’t the foundation. Here’s the stack you need to understand: 1. Core Principles Agents are: → Goal-driven → Autonomous → Able to perceive and reason → Capable of taking actions through tools → Able to adapt from outcomes and feedback 2. The Agent Loop Perceive → Reason → Plan → Act → Memory → Observe → Repeat Every weak link in this loop creates unreliable behavior. 3. Agent Types → Simple Reflex - rule-based responses → Goal-Based - works toward defined objectives → Utility-Based - chooses the best action → Learning Agent - improves through feedback → Multi-Agent - multiple agents working together 4. The Core Stack • LLM = Brain • Tools = Hands • Memory = Context • Knowledge = Information • Guardrails = Control 5. Building an Agent Define goal → Design workflow → Choose tools → Add memory → Add guardrails → Test → Deploy & monitor 6. Tools Orchestration: LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI Vector DBs: Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant Observability: LangSmith, Arize, W&B Deployment: Docker, Kubernetes, Modal 7. Measure What Matters • Task success • Accuracy • Cost & speed • Reliability • User satisfaction Treating Agentic AI like a framework problem. Master the principles first. Then choose the tools. Which part of the stack are you working on right now?
items.topicSummary: The post outlines a comprehensive stack for building agentic AI, emphasizing core principles, the agent loop, and key components before diving into tools. It highlights that mastering the foundational principles is crucial for production-ready agents, not just the framework.

items.author: AI For Professionals
items.comment: The distinction between governing static data and continuously monitoring AI behavior is crucial. For enterprise AI delivery, this implies that governance frameworks need to incorporate dynamic, real-time oversight mechanisms, moving beyond periodic policy reviews to ensure ongoing model integrity and defensibility.

commentSamples.text: Handing AI oversight to whoever runs the data team looks tidy on paper and falls apart in practice. Governance of behaviour asks a different skill set than governance of records, and that split forces an org chart change.

Disclosure rules for AI incidents are landing harder than most execs realised, and the reporting chain looks nothing like a data breach line. Serious calls also demand telling users when a machine handled them, which changes customer scripts overnight. …more
See more about the right tools for AI Governance at www.obsertd.com

Knowing where a number came from means nothing when nobody can explain why the machine picked it. Traceability of the decision itself is what regulators are asking for now, and most firms have not built anything that answers that.

Static policy documents cannot police a system that quietly shifts every night on new inputs. Board packs still show one snapshot per quarter while behaviour has already moved three times, and that gap is where accountability disappears.

Most boards treat AI oversight like a checkbox next to their data policy, and that split is where things break. Model drift happens overnight while written rules stay frozen, so the two need separate owners with separate teeth.

items.evidenceQuote: A data policy holds until you change it. A model drifts while you sleep.

items.text: Data Governance Is Not AI Governance 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝗻 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝟭 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝘆. 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗻𝗲𝘄𝘀𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱. 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝘂𝗽 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘄 → aiforleaders.com Original post: __________ If you think your data policy covers AI, you are wrong. Data governance asks whether the information is correct. AI governance asks whether the decision was defensible. Different questions. Different controls, different owners, different evidence. Here's where they split: → Data governance controls the input. AI governance controls the behaviour. → A data policy holds until you change it. A model drifts while you sleep. → Access control asks who may see the data. AI governance asks who may overrule the output. → Data lineage tells you where a number came from. Decision traceability tells you why the system chose it. → A breach gets reported to a data authority. A serious AI incident gets reported too, and people have to be told when they are dealing with AI. Every AI control assumes a data control underneath it. Which is exactly why AI governance is not an upgrade of data governance. It's a second layer that collapses without the first. Most SMEs are trying to build the second floor before the ground floor exists. Which of these six is open in your organisation right now? Credit to Alex Miguel Meyer. Follow him for more.
items.topicSummary: The post highlights six key differences between data governance and AI governance, emphasizing that AI governance is a distinct, second layer built upon data governance, not merely an extension.
items.whySelected: The point about model drift and the need for continuous monitoring is a practical implication for enterprise AI delivery, directly addressing the challenge of maintaining governance over evolving AI systems.

Lyza Valenzo As organizations introduce more AI tools, leaders have to think beyond productivity and prompts. *Who has access? *What information can employees put into these systems? *Which data is confidential? *How is identity managed? *What happens when a new tool introduces additional risk? *And who is responsible for making those decisions? items.text: As AI starts changing the way companies work, Wipro is taking a different approach to the fear of job losses. For Wipro, the bigger goal is not simply to make employees more productive, but to use that productivity for better business outcomes. items.text: 📖 A special package arrived today. I received my first author copy of The AI-Native Engineer Trail: A 60-Day Roadmap for Experienced Software Engineers & Architects from Amazon. There’s something different about holding a book in your hands after spending so much time turning ideas, notes, diagrams and experience into actual pages. This book started with a simple question: How should an experienced software engineer or architect navigate this new AI era without starting their career all over again? My answer became a 60-day trail - from models and prompting to agentic AI, context engineering, AI-native development, production AI, integration and building a portfolio. One idea runs throughout the book: You are not starting over. You are upgrading what you already know. AI can suggest. Experience decides. Seeing the physical copy for the first time makes this project feel very real. 😊 Sharing a few pictures of the author copy below. More to come. 🚀 hashtag #AINativeEngineer hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #SoftwareEngineering hashtag #SoftwareArchitecture hashtag #GenerativeAI hashtag #AIEngineering hashtag #Author
